Natural
NAT-u-ral
a.
From Latin naturalis, from natura, birth, nature, from nasci, to be born. Webster 1828: pertaining to nature; produced or effected by nature; not artificial. Paul uses it for the man as he is born, and the whole doctrine of depravity hangs on the adjective.

Biblical Definition

Paul’s contrast between two kinds of man turns on this word, and it is one of the most consequential adjectives in Scripture: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned (1 Corinthians 2:14). Three claims are made and each is stronger than the last: he does not receive, they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them. The impediment is not information but capacity, and the remedy therefore cannot be argument alone. The same adjective distinguishes the body sown from the body raised: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) — not matter against spirit, but the body animated by soul against the body animated by the Spirit. James uses it of a face in a mirror: the hearer who is not a doer is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass (James 1:23), who goes his way and forgets. And Paul uses natural for the created order in sexuality: even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature (Romans 1:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines NATURAL as pertaining to nature; produced or effected by nature, or by the laws of growth; not artificial; according to the stated course of things; and of persons, unregenerate, according to the state of man by birth.

NATURAL, a. — Pertaining to nature; produced or effected by nature, or by the laws of growth, formation or motion.

According to the stated course of things; not miraculous.

Not artificial or acquired; native; inborn; as natural affection.

Unaffected; unrestrained; without art; as a natural manner.

Latin naturalis, from natura, from nascor, to be born — the root of nation, native, nature.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 2:14 — "But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned."

1 Corinthians 15:44 — "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body."

James 1:23 — "For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass:"

Romans 1:26 — "For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature:"

Modern Corruption

1 Corinthians 2:14 says the natural man cannot know the things of God, which is the exact point at which every synergistic account of conversion must soften the verb.

expand to see more

Neither can he know them. Paul does not say the natural man will not, or is unlikely to, but that he cannot, and he gives the reason: the things of the Spirit are spiritually discerned, and the natural man has no such faculty. This is total depravity stated as an epistemological fact, and it is why the Reformed tradition holds that regeneration precedes faith rather than following upon it. A man dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1) is not persuaded into life; he is raised. Every scheme that makes the decisive movement the sinner’s own — whether classical Arminianism with its universal enabling grace or the revivalist technique that treats conversion as a decision to be induced — must at this verse make cannot mean something less than it says. The free offer of the gospel is not thereby weakened; God ordinarily gives life through the preached word, which is exactly why it is preached to all.

Romans 1:26 uses natural in its other and now contested sense: the created order, from which a departure is against nature. Paul’s argument is not from custom or majority practice but from creation — God made them male and female (Genesis 1:27; Matthew 19:4), and marriage is one man and one woman for life. The affirming readings of this passage (Vines, Brownson and others) proceed by restricting Paul to exploitative or idolatrous forms of the practice, and the text will not narrow that way: the ground given is nature itself, and the same chapter has just described the exchange of the truth of God for a lie. This dictionary holds that line while distinguishing sharply between pastoral care for image-bearers caught in sin and doctrinal affirmation of the sin. Every person addressed in Romans 1 bears the image of God, and Romans 2 immediately forbids the reader to feel superior.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek psuchikos (G5591), belonging to the soul, natural, sensual; phusikos (G5446), according to nature; genesis (G1078), birth or origin; phusis (G5449), nature.

expand to see more

Greek psuchikos (G5591) — of the soul, natural as opposed to spiritual; the natural man (1 Corinthians 2:14) and a natural body (1 Corinthians 15:44).

Greek pneumatikos (G4152) — spiritual, of the Spirit; the deliberate contrast in both passages.

Greek phusikos (G5446) — according to nature; the natural use (Romans 1:26-27).

Greek phusis (G5449) — nature, the constitution of a thing as created (Romans 1:26).

Greek genesis (G1078) — birth, origin; his natural face, literally the face of his birth (James 1:23).

Usage

"The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God... neither can he know them (1 Corinthians 2:14) — the impediment is capacity, not information."

"It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) — not matter against spirit, but two animating principles."

"Beholding his natural face in a glass (James 1:23) — the hearer who is not a doer, and forgets what he saw."
